Patient Information

Balance When the Problem Is Nerve or Muscle

A home programme for imbalance caused by peripheral neuropathy or muscle disease — training the senses that still work, and the muscles that still respond.

If your unsteadiness comes from the nerves in your legs or from the muscles themselves, the ordinary balance advice needs adjusting. The problem is not that your brain has forgotten how to balance. It is that the information reaching it, or the power leaving it, has been reduced — and a programme has to be built around that.

In neuropathy, the nerves that report where your feet and ankles are have become unreliable. Your brain is left balancing with two of its three senses. In myopathy, the sensing is intact but the muscles cannot produce the force to correct you in time. Both are trainable, but in different ways, and both have a few specific hazards that do not apply to anyone else.

What this programme can and cannot do

Balance training will not restore feeling in your feet, and no exercise regrows a damaged nerve quickly. What it does is teach your brain to lean harder on vision, on the inner ear and on light hand contact, and it builds the hip and calf strength that buys you time to correct. That is a real and worthwhile gain — and it is honest to say it is a workaround rather than a cure.

How to use this sheet
  • Read it once through, then start with the first two or three exercises only.
  • Add an exercise every week or two rather than starting everything at once.
  • Print it, tick off the days, and bring it back to your appointment.
  • This sheet is general information for my patients. If you have been given different, specific advice about your own condition, that advice comes first.
Before you start — making this safe to do alone
  • Always have something solid to grab. A kitchen bench, a heavy table, a wall on each side, or the back of a chair wedged against a wall. Not a wheeled chair, not a towel rail.
  • Choose the right floor. Bare, level, non-slip. Move rugs and cords out of the way. Do not do balance work on a rug edge or a wet bathroom floor.
  • Wear shoes or bare feet, not socks. Well-fitting shoes with a firm heel counter and a thin sole let you feel the floor.
  • If you have fallen in the last six months, or you feel unsafe standing still with your feet together, do not start alone. Do these first with a family member present, or ask me to arrange a physiotherapist.
  • Carry your phone, or wear a personal alarm, if you live alone.
  • Stop and contact your doctor if an exercise causes chest pain, sudden severe dizziness, a new weakness, or a fall.
Extra rules that apply specifically to you
  • Never train with your eyes closed, or on any soft surface, without both hands on a fixed bench. This is where people with neuropathy fall at home.
  • Do not train barefoot if you have an active or healed foot ulcer, a significant foot deformity, or poor circulation — wear a well-fitting shoe instead.
  • Never use heat — hot water bottles, heat packs, foot spas, radiant heaters — on feet with reduced sensation, and never treat corns or calluses yourself.
  • Do not train to failure. In muscle disease, the correct target is 'somewhat hard' and stopping with two or three repetitions in reserve.
  • Stop and get help the same day for a hot, red or swollen foot, or for dark, red or cola-coloured urine after exercise.

Balance runs on three senses. You have lost one of them.

Understanding which one explains why your symptoms behave the way they do — and what the training is actually doing.

🦶 The feet (position sense)

Normally the dominant sense on firm ground. In large-fibre neuropathy this is the one that fails, which is why your balance is worst on carpet, sand, grass and gravel — surfaces where the signal was already poor.

👁️ Vision

The sense that takes over, which is why you are steady in a lit room and unsafe in the dark. It explains why turning the bathroom light on is not a small matter, and why your balance is worse when you are tired or your glasses are wrong.

👂 The inner ear

Usually the sense with most spare capacity. It can be trained to take on more work — but it is slower and cruder than the feet were, which is why quick corrections and uneven ground remain hard.

Part 1 — The three things that prevent most of the falls

Do these before, and alongside, any exercise. They matter more than the exercises do.

Night-time and darkness planning

Set it up once; check it every few months
Where these falls happen

Vision is doing the work your feet used to do. Take the light away and the system fails — which is why so many falls in neuropathy happen on the way to the toilet at 2 am.

  1. Put a plug-in sensor night light in the bedroom, the hallway and the bathroom. This is the single highest-value change on this page.
  2. Keep a torch and your phone within reach of the bed.
  3. Clear the entire route to the bathroom — no shoes, no charging cables, no pets' bowls, no low furniture. Do it once, properly, and keep it that way.
  4. Sit on the edge of the bed for a count of ten before standing, and stand for a count of ten before walking. Blood pressure and stiff ankles both need that moment.
  5. Consider slip-resistant slippers with a firm back kept beside the bed — not loose scuffs and not bare feet on tiles.
  6. If you are up more than twice a night, tell me. Nocturia is a strong, treatable falls risk factor, and so are the medications that cause it.
Make it harderAdd a grab rail beside the toilet and in the shower. An occupational therapist home visit is worth arranging if you have had any fall at night.
Make it easierStart with the night lights alone.
SafetyNever walk in the dark to avoid waking a partner. Falls in the dark are the ones that break hips.
Why it worksHome fall-hazard reduction reduces falls by around a quarter overall, and by considerably more — nearly 40% — in people already at high risk. Note that this benefit comes from an actual assessment and actual changes, not from a leaflet.

Light-touch training (the fingertip trick)

Use it as the support setting for every balance exercise
Substitution strategy

When your feet cannot report where you are in space, your hand can. Resting a fingertip on a surface steadies you dramatically — and it works through information, not through physical support.

  1. Stand at the bench in whatever balance position you are working on.
  2. Instead of gripping, rest one fingertip lightly on the surface — press no harder than you would to touch a soap bubble without popping it.
  3. Notice how much steadier you are. That steadiness is not coming from the strength of your finger; it is your brain using the contact to work out where your body is.
  4. Practise progressing between four settings: two hands gripping → one hand → one fingertip → hand hovering a centimetre above the bench.
  5. Move down a setting only when the current one is easy, and always keep the next setting up within reach.
Make it harderFingertip → hovering hand → no hand, always beside the bench.
Make it easierBack to whole-hand contact. There is no shame in it, and the training effect is nearly as good.
SafetyHovering is the highest-risk setting: keep the hand directly above the bench so that catching yourself takes no time at all.
Why it worksLight fingertip contact at forces under one newton — far too little to hold you up — substantially reduces body sway, including in people with peripheral neuropathy. This is also the argument for walking poles: two poles give the same information on both sides, and are often better than one stick.

The daily foot check

Every day, at the same time
Non-negotiable if sensation is reduced

If you cannot feel your feet, they cannot tell you when something is wrong. Your eyes have to do the job instead. This takes 30 seconds and prevents most serious foot problems.

  1. Every evening, look at the whole of both feet — top, sole, heel, and between every toe. Use a mirror on the floor, or your phone camera, if you cannot see the soles.
  2. You are looking for: redness, blisters, cuts, cracks, new hard skin, a change in colour, or anything wet.
  3. Feel the temperature of each foot with the back of your hand and compare the two.
  4. Check inside your shoes with your hand before you put them on — for a stone, a fold in the insole, or a protruding stitch.
  5. Never use hot water bottles, heat packs, foot spas or radiant heaters on feet you cannot feel, and never cut corns or calluses yourself.
Make it harderAdd an annual (or more frequent) podiatry review, which for people with diabetes is subsidised in Australia.
Make it easierIf you cannot see or reach your feet, ask someone else to check them, or make it a regular podiatry task.
SafetyA hot, red, swollen foot needs same-day assessment, even without a wound and even if it does not hurt. In diabetic neuropathy this can be an acute Charcot foot, and continuing to walk on it can destroy the joint.
Why it worksDaily foot self-examination is a standing recommendation of the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot. A persistent difference of more than about 2°C between the same spot on the two feet, on two consecutive days, is a recognised early warning worth acting on.

Part 2 — Strength

Three days a week, on non-consecutive days. Read the loading rule first — it governs everything below it.

How hard to push a diseased muscle

Effort 6–7 out of 10; never to failure
The rule that governs everything else

Two opposite mistakes are common: not exercising at all for fear of damage, and training to exhaustion. The evidence supports a clear middle path.

  1. Work at an effort you would rate about 6 or 7 out of 10 — 'somewhat hard'. You should finish each set feeling you could have done two or three more repetitions.
  2. Never train to failure, and never chase 'the burn'.
  3. Prefer lifting and pushing (concentric work) over slow lowering of heavy loads (eccentric work). If you have a muscular dystrophy, actively avoid heavy eccentric work: no downhill hiking on steep gradients, no jumping, no slowly lowering heavy weights.
  4. Leave at least one rest day between sessions for the same muscle group — two or three sessions a week, not daily.
  5. Judge the last session by how you feel two days later: normal training soreness settles within 24 to 48 hours.
  6. Halve the load if soreness is severe, lasts beyond 72 hours, or comes with swelling — do not push through it.
Make it harderAdd repetitions before adding load. When you can comfortably do 15 repetitions at a given effort, add a small amount of weight and return to 10.
Make it easierReduce range, then repetitions, then frequency — in that order.
SafetyStop and seek urgent medical care if your urine turns dark, red or cola-coloured after exercise, which suggests muscle breakdown. If you have a metabolic muscle disease (such as McArdle disease or a fatty-acid oxidation disorder), never exercise fasted, take carbohydrate beforehand, warm up gently, and stop immediately if a muscle cramps and will not release — that is a contracture, not fatigue, and pushing through it is what causes damage.
Why it worksThe old fear of 'overwork weakness' comes largely from post-polio observation and a mouse model, not from human trials. Moderate resistance and aerobic training has repeatedly proved safe in inclusion body myositis, limb-girdle and Becker dystrophy and inflammatory myopathy, with no rise in muscle enzymes or biopsy inflammation. A Cochrane review classifies the benefit as low-certainty — safe, probably helpful, not miraculous. The genuine exceptions are high-force eccentric loading in the dystrophies and unpaced exertion in metabolic myopathy.

Sit-to-stand endurance test and training

Test monthly; train 3 days a week
Track your own progress

A simple number you can measure at home, repeat monthly, and bring to your appointment. It tracks exactly the muscles that fail first in myopathy — the thigh and hip.

  1. The test: sit on a firm dining chair, arms folded across your chest. Time how many complete stands you can do in 30 seconds. Write down the number and the date.
  2. If you cannot stand without using your arms, record that instead — 'five stands in 30 seconds with hands on thighs' is a perfectly good baseline.
  3. The training: do 3 sets of as many stands as you can comfortably manage in 30 seconds, resting a full minute between sets, three days a week.
  4. Keep the chair against a wall and stop each set with two or three repetitions still in reserve.
  5. Retest on the first of each month, under the same conditions.
Make it harderFewer arm assists, then a lower seat, then a slower lowering phase, then holding a light weight against the chest.
Make it easierUse a higher chair or a cushion, and push off your thighs.
SafetyChair against a wall. If you have inclusion body myositis, be aware that the knees can buckle without warning — keep a hand within reach of the bench for every set.
Why it worksIn limb-girdle and Becker dystrophy, twelve weeks of moderate resistance training improved sit-to-stand and stair times by roughly 18–36%, with no evidence of damage. In inclusion body myositis, training maintained quadriceps strength over three months while untrained controls lost around 9%.

Heel raises (calf strength)

10–15 repetitions × 2 sets, 3 days a week
Otago exercise

The calf is the engine of push-off in walking and the first muscle that catches you when you sway forwards.

  1. Stand at the bench, feet hip-width apart, hands resting on it for balance only.
  2. Rise up onto the balls of both feet as high as you can.
  3. Pause for a second at the top — most people cheat this part.
  4. Lower slowly, taking about 3 seconds, until your heels touch the floor.
  5. Repeat 10 to 15 times.
Make it harderFingertip support only. Then single-leg heel raises (holding the bench), building to 10 each side. Then do them with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step so the heel drops below the step — only with a solid rail.
Make it easierSmaller range, both hands on the bench, and do them seated first if standing is unsteady.
SafetyIf you get calf cramps, reduce the number and stretch afterwards. Stop if you get sudden calf pain and swelling — that needs assessment.
Why it worksCalf strength and ankle power decline steeply with age and correlate closely with walking speed, which itself predicts falls, hospitalisation and independence.

Standing leg raises — front, side and back

10 raises in each of the 3 directions, each leg, 3 days a week
Strength + balance in one

Strengthens the hip muscles (particularly the side-hip muscles that stop your pelvis dropping) while forcing you to balance on the other leg. Two exercises for the price of one.

  1. Stand tall behind a firm chair or at the bench, hands resting on it.
  2. Front: keeping the knee straight and the body upright, lift one leg forward about 20–30 cm. Lower slowly under control. Repeat 10 times.
  3. Side: lift the same leg directly out to the side, toes pointing forwards (not turned out), 20–30 cm. Do not lean away — the trick is to keep your trunk vertical. Lower slowly. Repeat 10 times.
  4. Back: lift the leg straight behind you, squeezing the buttock, without arching your low back or leaning forwards. Repeat 10 times.
  5. Swap legs and repeat all three directions.
  6. If your balance on the standing leg is poor, do all three directions lying on your side and on your back instead — you get most of the strengthening effect and none of the risk.
Make it harderReduce hand support to fingertips. Then add a 2-second hold at the top of each raise. Then add a light ankle weight (start at 0.5–1 kg) for the side and back raises.
Make it easierDo them seated for the front raises, and do side and back raises with both hands firmly on the bench and a smaller range.
SafetySlow and controlled beats high. A 20 cm raise done with a still trunk builds far more than a 50 cm raise done by swinging and leaning. If your sensation is reduced, keep both hands on the bench for these until the movement is second nature — you cannot rely on your feet to tell you that you are drifting.
Why it worksAnkle-weighted hip and knee exercises are the strength backbone of the Otago programme, which cut falls by roughly a third (rate ratio 0.68) across seven trials, and which also reduced falls in people referred to a falls clinic after an injury.

Step-ups on the bottom stair

5–10 step-ups each leg, 2 sets, 3 days a week
Power + confidence

Rebuilds the leg power you need for stairs, kerbs and buses, and rehearses the exact task people become frightened of.

  1. Use the bottom step of a staircase with a solid handrail, or a sturdy step block.
  2. Hold the rail. Place one whole foot on the step.
  3. Push down through that heel to lift yourself up — try to let the leg on the step do the work rather than pushing off the floor with the back foot.
  4. Step back down slowly, leading with the same leg, and touch down quietly.
  5. Do 10 with that leg, then swap.
Make it harderLight fingertip contact on the rail; then a slower 3-second lowering; then a higher step (only with a rail).
Make it easierA single low step or a thick book taped down; or start by simply stepping up and down onto a doorway threshold.
SafetyHandrail in hand for every repetition until you are certain. Shoes on. With reduced sensation, look at your foot as you place it on the step, every single time — do not place it by feel.
Why it worksStair negotiation demands more strength than walking and is where a lot of serious falls occur, so it is worth training deliberately rather than avoiding.

Part 3 — Balance, adapted

Same exercises as the general programme, with the support settings turned up and the progressions taken more slowly.

Weight shifts and reaching

10 shifts in each direction, daily
Starting point

Teaches you where your limits of balance actually are, and how to move to the edge of them and come back without panicking.

  1. Stand at the bench, feet hip-width apart, hands lightly resting on it.
  2. Keeping your body straight like a tall mast, sway slowly forwards over your toes, then back over your heels. Go only as far as you can come back from.
  3. Do ten of those, then sway slowly side to side, taking your weight over one foot then the other, ten times.
  4. Then reach one hand slowly out to the side and across your body, following your hand with your eyes, and return.
  5. Finish by reaching down towards a spot on the floor beside your foot and back up.
Make it harderReduce hand support; increase how far you reach; reach to place and pick up an object on a low stool.
Make it easierDo it seated on a firm chair first, or with both hands on the bench and very small movements.
SafetySmall ranges first. The point is control, not distance.
Why it worksReaching while standing is one of the functional balance tasks named in the 2022 World Falls Guidelines, and it directly rehearses the movements that cause household falls.

Tandem and semi-tandem standing

3 × 30 seconds each foot in front, daily
Foundation

The static version of tandem walking — the safest way to start if walking heel-to-toe is still too much.

  1. Stand beside a kitchen bench with one hand resting on it.
  2. Put one foot half a step in front of the other, heel beside the opposite big toe (semi-tandem).
  3. Hold for 30 seconds, breathing normally, eyes ahead.
  4. Swap which foot is in front and repeat.
  5. When 30 seconds is comfortable, move the front foot fully in front (true tandem) so heel touches toe.
Make it harderWhole hand → one hand → one fingertip → hovering hand. Progress the support, not the eyes. Do not attempt eyes closed in tandem stance at home.
Make it easierFeet together, both hands on the bench, 30 seconds.
SafetyStand facing into the corner of a bench, not out into the room, so there is something to catch on either side. Keep the light on. Practising in dim light is not a useful challenge for you — it is simply dangerous.
Why it worksFeet-together, semi-tandem and tandem stance are the standard progression used in the Otago programme and in nearly every trial that reduced falls.

Single-leg standing

Build to 15–30 seconds each leg, 2 rounds, daily, with hand support
Otago exercise

Almost every step you take is a moment of standing on one leg. This trains the hip and ankle muscles that stop you toppling sideways.

  1. Stand at the bench with both hands on it.
  2. Shift your weight fully onto one leg and lift the other foot a few centimetres off the floor — just enough to clear it.
  3. Keep the standing knee soft, hips level, and look at a fixed point ahead.
  4. Hold as long as you can steadily, up to 30 seconds, then swap.
  5. Do two rounds on each leg.
Make it harderTwo fingers on the bench → one finger → hands hovering just above it. Then add slow head turns, or stand on a firm cushion.
Make it easierKeep the toes of the lifted foot resting lightly on the floor (a 'kickstand'), taking almost no weight.
SafetyAlways within arm's reach of support. Do not test yourself in the middle of the room to 'see how long you can last'. If you have inclusion body myositis, the knee can give way without warning — keep a hand on the bench for every repetition, no exceptions.
Why it worksSingle-leg stance time is one of the balance tests used to decide who needs a falls intervention. Being unable to hold it for 10 seconds is a marker worth telling me about — it has been linked to higher mortality and to injurious falls, though it is a warning light rather than a target in itself.

Tandem walking (heel-to-toe), corridor only

10 steps × 2, once a day
Core balance drill

Trains the side-to-side balance control that keeps you upright when you turn, step around something, or are jostled.

  1. Do this in a corridor narrow enough that you can touch both walls with your elbows out, or beside a kitchen bench. Never in the middle of a room.
  2. Stand at one end with your fingertips lightly brushing one wall.
  3. Place one foot directly in front of the other so the heel of the front foot touches the toes of the back foot, as if walking a tightrope.
  4. Take ten slow heel-to-toe steps, looking ahead at a point on the wall rather than at your feet.
  5. Turn around carefully — wide, slow steps, not a quick pivot — and walk back.
  6. Rest, then repeat twice more.
Make it harderReduce from whole hand to fingertips on the wall. Do not progress to no hands, to head turns, or to walking backwards heel-to-toe unless a physiotherapist has assessed you.
Make it easierWalk with one whole hand on the wall, and use a semi-tandem step (front heel beside the back toes, not in front of them) until that feels steady.
SafetyNever in an open room, never on a rug, never in socks. If you find yourself repeatedly grabbing the wall, the drill is too hard — go back a stage. Corridor with two reachable walls, well lit, shoes on. Semi-tandem is a perfectly good end point if full tandem never becomes steady.
Why it worksNarrowing your base of support is the most efficient way to challenge balance, and challenging balance is what makes falls prevention work. In the Cochrane review of 108 trials, exercise reduced the rate of falls by 23% overall — but programmes that genuinely challenged balance and totalled three or more hours a week reduced falls by around 40%. Comfortable, seated, low-dose programmes did not.

Training the inner ear to take over (carefully)

3 × 15 seconds, feet apart, both hands down, every second day
Advanced — read the safety note

With your eyes open, vision does most of the work and the damaged system stays lazy. Closing your eyes forces the inner ear and the sensation in your feet to take over — which is how they improve.

  1. Stand in a corner, or facing into the corner of a kitchen bench, so support is available on both sides. Have someone nearby the first time.
  2. Stage 1: feet together, eyes open, 30 seconds. Then eyes closed, 30 seconds.
  3. Stage 2: semi-tandem (one heel beside the other big toe), eyes open then closed.
  4. Stage 3: full tandem (heel to toe), eyes open then closed.
  5. Stage 4: repeat the whole sequence standing on a firm sofa cushion or folded pillow, which removes reliable information from your feet as well.
  6. Move to the next stage only when you can hold the current one for 30 seconds without touching down.
Make it harderIncrease the time before you narrow the feet. Never combine a narrow stance with closed eyes at home.
Make it easierDo it with your eyes open in a dim room instead — you get some of the same effect with far less risk.
SafetyNever with your eyes closed in an open room. Corner or bench, every time. This is the highest-risk exercise on the page for you. Both hands stay on the bench throughout, feet stay hip-width apart, and someone should be in the house. If in doubt, skip it — the rest of the programme works without it.
Why it worksBalance training that systematically removes vision and reliable foot sensation is a core recommendation in the vestibular hypofunction guideline, alongside gaze stabilisation.

Part 4 — Conditioning

The part that protects against becoming weaker for reasons that have nothing to do with your diagnosis.

Steady aerobic exercise

20–30 minutes at a moderate pace, 3 days a week
Safe and worthwhile

Nerve and muscle disease make everyday activity more expensive in energy terms, so people become deconditioned quickly — and deconditioning then gets blamed on the disease. Aerobic training treats the part that is reversible.

  1. A stationary bike is the best choice: it is seated, it removes the falls risk, and the resistance is easy to control. Walking, swimming or water walking also work well.
  2. Work at a pace where you can talk in short sentences but not sing — around 60–65% of your maximum heart rate.
  3. Start with 10 minutes if that is where you are, and add 2–3 minutes per week.
  4. Warm up for 5 minutes at a very easy pace and cool down the same way, which matters more in muscle disease than in healthy muscle.
  5. Pace it: it is better to do 20 minutes three times a week than 60 minutes once and then need three days to recover.
Make it harderAdd duration first, then a little intensity. Interval formats (2 minutes harder, 3 minutes easy) suit people who fatigue quickly.
Make it easierSplit into two 10-minute sessions. Water-based exercise offloads the joints and the falls risk together.
SafetyIn metabolic myopathies, avoid sudden high-intensity bursts and never exercise fasted. Stop for chest pain, unusual breathlessness, or muscle pain that is sharp rather than tired.
Why it worksSubmaximal cycling has been shown to be safe and effective in limb-girdle dystrophy and in mitochondrial myopathy, with meaningful gains in aerobic capacity and no significant rise in muscle enzymes. In early diabetic neuropathy, sustained aerobic exercise over a year has even been associated with an increase in small nerve fibre density in the skin — the one intervention with any evidence of a structural nerve effect.

Walking — the background to everything else

Build towards 30 minutes on most days
Aerobic base

Walking will not by itself fix your balance, but it maintains leg strength, bone, mood, sleep and blood pressure control, and it is the platform the rest of the programme sits on.

  1. Start from where you actually are. If that is five minutes to the letterbox and back, start there.
  2. Add roughly 10% per week — an extra two or three minutes.
  3. Walk at a pace where you could talk but not sing.
  4. Take a route you can shorten easily if you tire: laps of a level block beat a one-way walk you have to complete.
  5. If you are unsteady, walk with someone, or use walking poles or your stick — using an aid is not a failure, it is what allows you to do more.
Make it harderAdd a hill, add pace intervals (two minutes brisk, two minutes easy), or add uneven ground such as a grassy park — but only once your balance work is solid.
Make it easierSplit it into three 10-minute walks. Indoor shopping-centre laps are a legitimate winter option.
SafetyDo not do your balance-challenging exercises outdoors on uneven ground unsupervised. Check your feet after every longer walk, and check inside your shoes before it.
Why it worksBe clear about this: walking alone has not been shown to prevent falls, and across 88 trials the programmes that included walking training had smaller effects on falls than those that did not. Walking is essential for fitness, mood, bone and nerve health. It is not a substitute for the balance work above.

Things people are told that are not true

"Exercising a weak muscle will wear it out permanently."

This is the 'overwork weakness' idea, and it comes largely from observations after polio and from a mouse model — not from human trials. Moderate resistance training has been studied in inclusion body myositis, limb-girdle and Becker muscular dystrophy and inflammatory myopathy, and it improved or maintained strength without raising muscle enzymes or inflammation on biopsy.

The nuance that does survive is narrow but real: avoid heavy eccentric loading (slowly lowering heavy weights, steep downhill walking, jumping) if you have a muscular dystrophy, and avoid unpaced, all-out exertion if you have a metabolic muscle disease.

"My CK went up, so the exercise is damaging my muscles."

Creatine kinase rises modestly after unaccustomed exercise in almost everyone. In the training trials it did not rise significantly, and where it did there was no accompanying loss of function. Your symptoms, your function and the colour of your urine are far more useful safety monitors than a single CK level.

"If I can't feel my feet I shouldn't be walking on them."

Weight-bearing exercise was formally discouraged in diabetic neuropathy for decades. A randomised trial of a walking programme found no increase in foot ulcers, and the advice was reversed. What is required is the footwear, the daily foot check and prompt attention to any break in the skin — not inactivity.

"Balance training will bring the feeling back in my feet."

It will not, and I would rather you knew that at the start. It trains substitution — vision, the inner ear, hip strength and hand contact. The only intervention with any evidence of a structural effect on small nerve fibres is sustained aerobic exercise over about a year, mostly in people whose neuropathy is early or not yet established.

"Wobble boards and balance cushions are the proper way to train."

For someone with proprioceptive loss they are the worst possible choice for unsupervised use: an unstable surface is precisely where you have no capacity to correct. They are clinic tools, used with a therapist beside you. The home version is a folded towel with both hands on the bench, once everything on firm ground is easy.

"Using poles or a stick means giving in."

A hand resting on a stable surface reduces body sway even at pressures far too light to hold you up — the hand is supplying the position information your feet no longer can. Two poles give that on both sides and are often better than a single stick. This is physiology, not weakness.

"Textured or vibrating insoles will fix my balance."

The evidence is thin and mixed — around a 5% change in sway in one small trial, and other studies show textured insoles slowing walking. Spend the money on good shoes and a night light instead.

If you do fall: the plan you make in advance

Long lies on the floor cause far more harm than the fall itself. Rehearse this before you need it.

1

Do not rush to get up

Lie still for a moment. Check whether anything hurts badly, and whether you can move both arms and both legs. If you suspect a broken bone, or you hit your head, or you are on blood thinners, call for help and stay where you are.

2

Roll, crawl, kneel, rise

Roll onto your side, then onto your hands and knees. Crawl to a solid chair or a bed. Put both hands on the seat, bring your strongest leg up so that foot is flat on the floor, then push up through that leg and both arms and turn to sit.

3

If you cannot get up

Get to a warm place if you can — drag a blanket or cushion down. Keep moving your arms and legs to protect your skin and circulation. Bang on a wall or floor. This is exactly what a personal alarm pendant is for, and why it must be worn rather than left on the bedside table.

4

Tell me about it

Every fall is worth reporting, even one you were not hurt by. A fall is the single strongest predictor of the next fall, and most causes are treatable — blood pressure medication, vision, inner ear, sensation in the feet, or simple loss of leg strength.

Being honest about the evidence: teaching people to get up off the floor is widely recommended on the strength of the harm caused by long lies — about half of uninjured people who fall cannot get up unaided, and pressure injury, dehydration, muscle breakdown, hypothermia and pneumonia all follow from lying there. The trials that have tested floor-rise training are small and have not shown a clear change in the ability to rise. Rehearse it anyway: the cost is five minutes and the plan itself is worth having.
Hurt is not the same as harm

Muscles that have worked will ache. As a rule of thumb, discomfort up to about 4 or 5 out of 10 during and after exercise is acceptable, provided it settles back to your normal level within 24 hours and is not getting worse week on week. Sharp, sudden or one-sided pain is a reason to stop.

Making it actually happen

The best programme is the one you will still be doing in three months. These are the things that reliably make the difference.

🔗 Attach it to something you already do

Balance work while the kettle boils. Neck exercises after brushing your teeth. Relaxation practice as you get into bed. A new habit hooked onto an old one survives; a new habit floating free does not.

📅 Keep a tick sheet

A calendar on the fridge with a tick for each day. Self-monitoring is one of the few adherence strategies with consistent evidence behind it, and it gives us something real to look at in clinic.

🎯 Set a specific, checkable goal

Not 'improve my balance', but 'stand on one leg for 30 seconds each side by the end of March', or 'walk to the shops and back without stopping'. Write it down.

⏱️ Ten minutes beats an hour you never start

Short daily sessions beat one long weekly effort. The programmes below are designed to be done in ten to twenty minutes, most days, in your own kitchen or hallway.

Almost every trial that produced a real result ran for at least eight to twelve weeks. Judge the programme at three months, not at three days.

Getting extra help in Australia

You do not have to do this alone, and supervised programmes work better than unsupervised ones for people at higher risk.

🩺 Your GP can subsidise allied health

Since 1 July 2025, GP Management Plans and Team Care Arrangements have been replaced by the GP Chronic Condition Management Plan. With one in place, you can access up to five Medicare-rebated allied health services per calendar year — shared across all disciplines, so five physiotherapy sessions means none left for anything else (ten services for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients). Referral is now by an ordinary letter rather than a special form. Ask your GP whether you are eligible.

🏃 Physiotherapist or exercise physiologist

A physiotherapist is the right choice for a specific problem — a painful neck, an unsteady gait, vestibular rehabilitation. An accredited exercise physiologist is the right choice for building and supervising a long-term conditioning programme. Both can be seen privately without a referral.

👥 Community falls programmes

NSW Health and many local councils run group strength-and-balance programmes such as Stepping On. Group programmes add the two things a home sheet cannot: supervision and company. Ask your GP or your local council, or search Active and Healthy NSW.

🏠 My Aged Care and NDIS

If you are over 65 and finding daily tasks harder, a My Aged Care assessment can fund home exercise support, home modifications such as rails, and an occupational therapy home-safety visit. Under 65 with a permanent disability, the same supports may be available through the NDIS.

Contact me, or seek urgent care, if
  • Your foot becomes hot, red or swollen, with or without pain and with or without a wound — same-day assessment.
  • Your urine turns dark, red or cola-coloured after exercise — this needs urgent assessment. Do not take ibuprofen or similar anti-inflammatories for post-exercise muscle pain if you have a metabolic muscle disease.
  • A muscle cramps during exercise and will not release within seconds — stop immediately.
  • You develop any break in the skin, blister or new callus on a foot with reduced sensation.
  • Your balance or strength deteriorates quickly, over days or weeks. That is not a training problem — it needs re-examination.
  • You develop new difficulty swallowing, or your legs give way without warning.
  • Muscle soreness is severe, lasts beyond 72 hours, or comes with visible swelling.
